messages.author: 1c17aa244a7a9832
messages.subject: Evenly distributed data
parts:
Hi all,

Thank you for providing such fantastic online resources and for all the help you have already provided on this list. I am a PhD student at Manchester Metropolitan University researching the population density and abundance of Northern lesser galagos (Galago senegalensis) in Senegal (37 transects; range: 554–4519 m) and Kenya (1059 transects; range: 1059–11765m) alongside my colleagues at MMU. We are analysing the data from the two populations separately.


We segmented the data from both populations using the ‘rule of thumb’ (2 x truncation distance). This created 512 segments of roughly 160 m in length for Sengal and 506 segments of roughly 200 m in length for Kenya. We then ran simple dsms (no covariates), which seemed to work well for the Kenya data (~49 % deviance explained) but only ~4 % deviance was explained for the dsm on the Senegal data. The Senegal data is much more evenly distributed than the Kenya data – could that be the reason for the poor model in Senegal? We tried other distributions (eg. tweedie) and there was no improvement. We’ve increased the segment size from 160m (2 x truncation distance of 80m) to 300m for the Senegal data and there is a slight improvement but not much difference.


Any advice you have that could improve the performance of the model(s) would be much appreciated.


All the best,

Grace

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Evenly distributed data
parts:
Grace

Could you clarify your comment about dsms without covariates explaining 49% and 4% of deviance in your respective datasets?  Do you mean the dsms had x,y (spatial coordinates) as covariates but nothing else?

Assuming that is what you meant, the results are consistent with spatial variability for the Kenya data being explicable by space alone whereas space only had little explanatory ability with the Senegal data.
